parameters.label: Hours since the workout
parameters.explain: Soreness isn't there at once: it builds over hours and is worst a day or two later.

parameters.label: First time or repeat
parameters.explain: The first hard workout teaches the muscle to protect itself, so the same workout later causes much less soreness.

parameters.label: How hard the workout was
parameters.explain: Working muscles harder than they're used to causes more tiny tears.

parameters.label: Lowering movements
parameters.explain: Muscles lengthening under load — lowering into a squat, running downhill — cause the most soreness.

overlay.caption: tiny tears → repair over days → soreness peaks, then fades

explain.summary: Marcus worked his leg muscles harder than they were used to, which made tiny tears in the muscle fibres. Repairing them takes days, and the soreness builds slowly — fine on Monday night, worst around Wednesday, gone by the weekend. The first workout also teaches the muscle to protect itself, so the same workout next week hurts much less.
rules: Soreness builds over the first day and peaks about 1–2 days after the workout.
It fades over the next few days and is nearly gone by day 5.
Harder workouts and lots of lowering movements make it stronger.
Doing the same workout again causes much less soreness.

source.fact: Delayed soreness starts one to three days after a workout and builds over several hours; it rarely lasts more than five days.
It comes from tiny tears in muscle fibres when muscles are worked too hard, especially with a new workout.
Lengthening movements under load (eccentric movements) are the most likely to cause it.
One bout of lengthening exercise produces an adaptation that reduces damage and soreness in later bouts, lasting at least six months.

choice.what: Soreness follows a rise-and-fall curve that peaks around 40 hours
choice.why: This matches 'starts 1–3 days later, rarely lasts more than five days'. The exact peak differs between people.

choice.what: A repeat workout gives 60% less soreness
choice.why: Studies show much less soreness the second time; 60% is a round teaching value.

choice.what: Repair is shown as a smooth percentage
choice.why: Real repair has several overlapping stages; one curve keeps it simple.

illustrative: Marcus's very hard first workout and his 8-out-of-10 soreness on Wednesday are made up for a fictional story.
The 0–10 soreness scale is a teaching scale.

citations.title: Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness (DOMS)
citations.supports: DOMS starts one to three days after a workout and builds over several hours; it rarely lasts more than five days; it comes from tiny tears in muscle fibers after working muscles too hard, especially with new workouts and lengthening (eccentric) movements.

citations.title: How long does the protective effect on eccentric exercise-induced muscle damage last? (Med Sci Sports Exerc)
citations.publisher: MRC Protein Phosphorylation and Ubiquitylation Unit, University of Dundee (publication record)
citations.supports: Abstract: one bout of eccentric exercise produces an adaptation that reduces muscle damage, including soreness, in later bouts; the protection lasts at least 6 months.

does: Shows soreness arriving late, peaking about two days after a hard workout, then fading
Shows harder and lowering-heavy workouts causing more soreness
Shows the same workout causing less soreness the second time
doesnt: Tell the difference between normal soreness and an injury
Say how anyone should train or what to eat
limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: Normal soreness is dull and fades in a few days. Sharp pain, swelling or pain that gets worse is a reason to stop and tell a coach or adult.
